summary: Earth Jukebox is a website that turns NASA pictures into sound. You can choose images of city lights, ocean currents, or carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. The app scans each picture from left to right. Bright areas make louder sounds, and areas near the top make higher notes. You can change the sound settings, save tracks in a playlist, and download the audio. A moving line shows which part of the picture you are hearing. This gives people another way to explore NASA images. The audio is based on the picture’s pixels, so labels and backgrounds affect it too.
details:
How the sound works

The app scans a picture from left to right. Bright pixels make louder sounds. Pixels near the top play higher notes than pixels near the bottom. A line moves across the picture during playback so you can follow what you are hearing. The sound score shows the brightness values used to make the audio.

What you can do

Choose from three NASA images: night lights, ocean currents, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Generate a track, listen, and change the settings. You can adjust the track length, pitch range, and how brightness affects the sound. You can also make dark areas louder instead of bright areas.

Add tracks to a playlist, give them names and notes, change their order, and play them together. Playlists stay in your browser when you return. You can download the sound as a WAV file. You can also export a playlist file and import it in another browser. That file saves the image choices and settings, then the app makes the sound again.

Why use it

The goal is to give people another way to explore NASA pictures through sight and sound. The picture, moving line, and audio stay connected. The app has keyboard controls, image descriptions, listening instructions, and reduced-motion support. It has not been tested in a formal accessibility study.

Tools and sources

The website uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. A browser worker makes the audio. Node.js is used for the local server and tests. FFmpeg was used to sample the pictures. The layout uses the Bootstrap Album template. The sound method comes from SpectroTrace by Jonathan About, with its MIT license and credits kept in the app.

The three pictures come from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio pages 5313, 3912, and 5196. The original pictures are included without visual changes. Their source links are listed below.

What the sound means

The audio comes from picture pixels, including colors, labels, and backgrounds. It does not measure temperature or carbon dioxide levels. The scan moves across space in the picture, not through years of data. Each track’s volume is adjusted separately, so a louder track does not mean a larger environmental value.

AI use

OpenAI Codex helped with research, code, debugging, tests, layout, and writing. The pictures come from NASA. The audio is made by the credited sound algorithm. The app does not train or run an AI model.
